We corroborate this pattern with experiments in pretrained language models. Finally, in the toy setting we observe a two-phase learning dynamic: networks first memorize individual factual associations in a few steps, then -- over a longer horizon -- learn to linearly separate true from false, which in turn lowers language-modeling loss. Together, these results provide both a mechanistic demonstration and an empirical motivation for how and why linear truth representations can emerge in language models.

papers.title: Large Language Models Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs' internal states reflect truthfulness or merely the process of recalling parametric knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs' internal states encode the process of knowledge recall, not truthfulness, making hallucination detection challenging for associated hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: Hidden states encode whether models rely on their parametric knowledge rather than truthfulness, so detection methods succeed for unassociated hallucinations but struggle for associated hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Associated Hallucinations (AHs) and Factual Associations (FAs) share similar internal processes and representational geometries.
Existing hallucination detection methods struggle to distinguish AHs from FAs, performing near random guessing.
Unassociated Hallucinations (UHs) are more separable in representation space and can be reliably detected.
Refusal tuning is less effective for AHs due to representational overlap with FAs, while it works better for UHs.
Subject popularity in pre-training data correlates with the prevalence of AHs and FAs, but not with UHs.
papers.limitation:
Focus on factual knowledge, not long-form or open-ended generation tasks
Lack of analysis on prompt-based hallucination detection approaches
Applicability limited to open-source LLMs, not black-box or large reasoning models
future_direction: Future evaluations should report detection performance separately for Associated Hallucinations and Unassociated Hallucinations.
Integrate LLMs with external feedback mechanisms, such as fact-checking modules or retrieval-based verifiers.
Prioritize improving detection of Associated Hallucinations due to their higher risk in practical deployments.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) encode factuality signals in their internal representations, such as hidden states, attention weights, or token probabilities, implying that LLMs may "know what they don't know". However, LLMs can also produce factual errors by relying on shortcuts or spurious associations. These error are driven by the same training objective that encourage correct predictions, raising the question of whether internal computations can reliably distinguish between factual and hallucinated outputs. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic analysis of how LLMs internally process factual queries by comparing two types of hallucinations based on their reliance on subject information. We find that when hallucinations are associated with subject knowledge, LLMs employ the same internal recall process as for correct responses, leading to overlapping and indistinguishable hidden-state geometries. In contrast, hallucinations detached from subject knowledge produce distinct, clustered representations that make them detectable. These findings reveal a fundamental limitation: LLMs do not encode truthfulness in their internal states but only patterns of knowledge recall, demonstrating that "LLMs don't really know what they don't know".

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: When Truth Is Overridden: Uncovering the Internal Origins of Sycophancy in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does sycophantic behavior arise within the internal mechanisms of Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Sycophancy in LLMs arises from a two-stage process in late layers: a preference shift towards the user's opinion and a deeper representational divergence, while user expertise claims are not internally encoded and thus have minimal impact.
papers.conclusion: Sycophancy is not a surface-level artifact but emerges from a structural override of learned knowledge in deeper layers, with implications for alignment and truthful AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
User opinions strongly induce sycophancy, while expertise framing has minimal impact.
Sycophancy emerges in two stages: a late-layer output preference shift and a deeper representational divergence.
Activation patching confirms the causal role of late-layer representations in sycophantic behavior.
Expertise levels are not encoded internally, as their representations overlap, unlike opinion prompts which form distinct clusters.
First-person prompts induce higher sycophancy than third-person prompts due to stronger representational perturbations in deeper layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophantic behavior, agreeing with user-stated opinions even when those contradict factual knowledge. While prior work has documented this tendency, the internal mechanisms that enable such behavior remain poorly understood. In this paper, we provide a mechanistic account of how sycophancy arises within LLMs. We first systematically study how user opinions induce sycophancy across different model families. We find that simple opinion statements reliably induce sycophancy, whereas user expertise framing has a negligible impact. Through logit-lens analysis and causal activation patching, we identify a two-stage emergence of sycophancy: (1) a late-layer output preference shift and (2) deeper representational divergence. We also verify that user authority fails to influence behavior because models do not encode it internally. In addition, we examine how grammatical perspective affects sycophantic behavior, finding that first-person prompts (``I believe...'') consistently induce higher sycophancy rates than third-person framings (``They believe...'') by creating stronger representational perturbations in deeper layers. These findings highlight that sycophancy is not a surface-level artifact but emerges from a structural override of learned knowledge in deeper layers, with implications for alignment and truthful AI systems.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: On the Generalizability of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals"
papers.research_question: Does the competition of mechanisms between factual recall and counterfactual repetition, as identified by Ortu et al. (2024), generalize to larger models, different prompt structures, and across domains?
papers.core_contribution: The attention head ablation method from Ortu et al. (2024) does not generalize well; its effectiveness varies significantly with model architecture, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.conclusion: The competition of mechanisms identified by Ortu et al. (2024) is not fully generalizable; experimental findings in mechanistic interpretability are highly dependent on the specific model, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.key_findings:
Successfully reproduced the original findings on GPT-2 small and Pythia 6.9B regarding positional information encoding, attention block dominance, and attention head specialization.
In Llama 3.1 8B, attention head specialization is greatly reduced, and the logit lens method shows limited early-layer activity and a sharp final-layer activation.
Changing the prompt structure to a question-answering format reduces the model's propensity to repeat the counterfactual, indicating sensitivity to repetition.
The choice of premise word (e.g., 'Redefine', 'Validate') affects the rate of factual vs. counterfactual predictions and the effectiveness of attention head ablation.
The effectiveness of the proposed attention head ablation varies across domains; it works best for domains where the factual token is leaked in the subject (e.g., 'Autos and Vehicles') and fails for others.
papers.limitation:
The logit lens method may be unreliable for larger models like Llama 3.1 8B, potentially failing to capture early-layer mechanisms.
The filtered MQuAKE dataset used for domain analysis is very small (228 prompts), limiting definitive conclusions.
Most extended findings rely on GPT-2 small and a dataset derived from Ortu et al. (2024), limiting generalizability to other models and datasets.
future_direction: Investigate whether larger models distribute work more evenly across heads or if newer interpretability techniques (e.g., circuit analysis, tuned lens) are needed to capture their mechanisms.
Conduct a deeper analysis of why certain dataset domains impact attention head activation, distinguishing between token leakage, topic words, and task difficulty.
Extend the findings to different, larger datasets and models, as well as new prompt structures and premise words.
papers.abstract: We present a reproduction study of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals" (Ortu et al., 2024), which investigates competition of mechanisms in language models between factual recall and counterfactual in-context repetition. Our study successfully reproduces their primary findings regarding the localization of factual and counterfactual information, the dominance of attention blocks in mechanism competition, and the specialization of attention heads in handling competing information. We reproduce their results on both GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) and Pythia 6.9B (Biderman et al., 2023). We extend their work in three significant directions. First, we explore the generalizability of these findings to even larger models by replicating the experiments on Llama 3.1 8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), discovering greatly reduced attention head specialization. Second, we investigate the impact of prompt structure by introducing variations where we avoid repeating the counterfactual statement verbatim or we change the premise word, observing a marked decrease in the logit for the counterfactual token. Finally, we test the validity of the authors' claims for prompts of specific domains, discovering that certain categories of prompts skew the results by providing the factual prediction token as part of the subject of the sentence. Overall, we find that the attention head ablation proposed in Ortu et al. (2024) is ineffective for domains that are underrepresented in their dataset, and that the effectiveness varies based on model architecture, prompt structure, domain and task.

papers.title: In Praise of Stubbornness: An Empirical Case for Cognitive-Dissonance Aware Continual Update of Knowledge in LLMs
papers.research_question: What happens when LLMs encounter contradictory information, and can selective plasticity help maintain knowledge integrity?
papers.core_contribution: Contradictory updates in LLMs cause catastrophic interference on unrelated knowledge, while non-contradictory updates are safe. Selective plasticity helps for non-contradictory updates but fails for contradictory ones. Contradictions can be detected with high accuracy using model features.
papers.conclusion: LLMs lack a contradiction filter, leading to catastrophic interference from contradictory updates. This motivates new architectures that can resist contradictions, possibly by incorporating cognitive dissonance detection, append-only updates, and selective plasticity.
papers.key_findings:
Contradictory updates cause catastrophic interference, destroying up to 80% of unrelated knowledge even with few contradicting facts.
Non-contradictory updates can be integrated safely with minimal forgetting.
Selective plasticity (avoiding stubborn neurons) improves retention for non-contradictory updates but fails for contradictory updates.
Contradictory information can be detected with >95% accuracy using internal or output model features.
The catastrophic interference from contradictory updates persists across model scales (GPT-2 to GPT-J-6B) and training methods.
papers.limitation:
The use of simple factual statements may not capture complex knowledge conflicts.
Contradiction detection generalizability to nuanced scenarios is untested.
Scale limitations: small tracked knowledge relative to model capacity, and unclear effects in larger commercial models.
future_direction: Explore architectures that incorporate cognitive dissonance detection, append-only updates, and selective plasticity.
Design dedicated datasets and benchmarks for conflict detection.
papers.abstract: Through systematic empirical investigation, we uncover a fundamental and concerning property of Large Language Models: while they can safely learn facts that don't contradict their knowledge, attempting to update facts with contradictory information triggers catastrophic corruption of unrelated knowledge. Unlike humans, who naturally resist contradictory information, these models indiscriminately accept contradictions, leading to devastating interference, destroying up to 80% of unrelated knowledge even when learning as few as 10-100 contradicting facts. To understand whether this interference could be mitigated through selective plasticity, we experiment with targeted network updates, distinguishing between previously used (stubborn) and rarely used (plastic) neurons. We uncover another asymmetry: while sparing frequently-used neurons significantly improves retention of existing knowledge for non-contradictory updates (98% vs 93% with standard updates), contradictory updates trigger catastrophic interference regardless of targeting strategy. This effect which persists across tested model scales (GPT-2 to GPT-J-6B), suggests a fundamental limitation in how neural networks handle contradictions. Finally, we demonstrate that contradictory information can be reliably detected (95%+ accuracy) using simple model features, offering a potential protective mechanism. These findings motivate new architectures that can, like humans, naturally resist contradictions rather than allowing destructive overwrites.

papers.title: Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do distributional and mechanistic factors determine a language model's behavior when there is a conflict between memorized facts and in-context information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies specific attention heads that control the use of memorized vs. in-context information and shows that scaling these heads at runtime can dynamically control model behavior without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that frequency and specific attention heads influence factual recall and provides a proof of concept for controlling model behavior dynamically at runtime.
papers.key_findings:
The frequency of the country and in-context city in pretraining data affects the model's tendency to use memorized vs. in-context information.
Larger models are more likely to use memorized answers, especially for frequent terms.
Individual attention heads can be identified that promote either memorized or in-context answers.
Scaling down a memory head can increase the rate of in-context answers to 88% on the world capitals task.
The memory head promotes geography-related tokens, indicating domain specificity, and does not generalize well to other factual domains.
papers.limitation: The dataset used is templated and limited to the domain of country-capital relationships, so findings may not generalize to arbitrary contexts.
future_direction: Developing more general techniques for controlling the use of context vs. memorized information in arbitrary tasks.
Discovering more general mechanisms beyond domain-specific heads.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often must integrate facts they memorized in pretraining with new information that appears in a given context. These two sources can disagree, causing competition within the model, and it is unclear how an LM will resolve the conflict. On a dataset that queries for knowledge of world capitals, we investigate both distributional and mechanistic determinants of LM behavior in such situations. Specifically, we measure the proportion of the time an LM will use a counterfactual prefix (e.g., “The capital of Poland is London”) to overwrite what it learned in pretraining (“Warsaw”). On Pythia and GPT2, the training frequency of both the query country (”Poland”) and the in-context city (”London”) highly affect the models’ likelihood of using the counterfactual. We then use head attribution to identify individual attention heads that either promote the memorized answer or the in-context answer in the logits. By scaling up or down the value vector of these heads, we can control the likelihood of using the in-context answer on new data. This method can increase the rate of generating the in-context answer to 88% of the time simply by scaling a single head at runtime. Our work contributes to a body of evidence showing that we can often localize model behaviors to specific components and provides a proof of concept for how future methods might control model behavior dynamically at runtime.

papers.title: A Glitch in the Matrix? Locating and Detecting Language Model Grounding with Fakepedia
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms underlying LLMs' ability to ground answers in contextual information that contradicts their parametric knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset, and MGCT, a causal mediation analysis method, to study grounding in LLMs, finding that grounding is a distributed process and that computational patterns can predict grounding behavior.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that grounding is a distributed process, ungrounded responses involve factual recall in MLPs, and grounding can be predicted from computation patterns, contributing to a coherent narrative of grounding and factual recall mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Grounding, contrary to factual recall, is a distributed process without clear localization.
The activity of a few MLPs differs significantly between grounded and ungrounded modes.
Computational patterns can predict whether a model is grounded with 92.8% accuracy.
Models exhibit diverse grounding behaviors; e.g., Mistral-7B is highly compliant while GPT-4 Turbo strongly prefers parametric knowledge.
Not grounding involves activating factual recall processes in the MLPs of the final subject token.
papers.limitation:
Descriptive analysis may be influenced by the choice of prompting strategy.
Mediation setup requires the object token to be the last token; different behaviors might emerge in other setups.
Automatic detection model may not generalize outside the experimental domain.
Does not distinguish between plausible and absurd counterfactual facts.
Dataset generation could be improved with interaction flows based on other language models as critics.
future_direction: Explore relationship between prompting strategy and grounding frequency.
Study grounding behavior in different experimental setups.
Investigate how grounding varies with the likelihood of counterfactual facts.
Improve dataset generation using language models as critics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have an impressive ability to draw on novel information supplied in their context. Yet the mechanisms underlying this contextual grounding remain unknown, especially in situations where contextual information contradicts factual knowledge stored in the parameters, which LLMs also excel at recalling. Favoring the contextual information is critical for retrieval-augmented generation methods, which enrich the context with up-to-date information, hoping that grounding can rectify outdated or noisy stored knowledge. We present a novel method to study grounding abilities using Fakepedia, a novel dataset of counterfactual texts constructed to clash with a model's internal parametric knowledge. In this study, we introduce Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset designed to evaluate grounding abilities when the internal parametric knowledge clashes with the contextual information. We benchmark various LLMs with Fakepedia and conduct a causal mediation analysis of LLM components when answering Fakepedia queries, based on our Masked Grouped Causal Tracing (MGCT) method. Through this analysis, we identify distinct computational patterns between grounded and ungrounded responses. We finally demonstrate that distinguishing grounded from ungrounded responses is achievable through computational analysis alone. Our results, together with existing findings about factual recall mechanisms, provide a coherent narrative of how grounding and factual recall mechanisms interact within LLMs.

papers.title: No Answer Needed: Predicting LLM Answer Accuracy from Question-Only Linear Probes
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a simple linear probe on residual stream activations can predict an LLM's forthcoming answer correctness, revealing a linearly separable 'factual correctness' signal that generalizes across knowledge domains but fails for mathematical reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The analysis advances understanding of how LLMs encode self-assessment, providing evidence for a general 'Factual Correctness' direction while highlighting the structural distinctness of reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
A correctness signal is linearly separable in the activation space and generalizes from trivia questions to other factual knowledge datasets.
The correctness direction fails to generalize to mathematical reasoning tasks (GSM8K), indicating a structural misalignment between factual and arithmetic correctness.
Linear separability of correctness is low in early layers and saturates at intermediate transformer layers.
For models that answer 'I don't know', doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, suggesting the same direction captures implicit confidence.
The in-advance correctness signal is strongest and most consistent for the largest model tested (Llama 3.3 70B).
papers.limitation: The learned correctness direction does not generalize to arithmetic-reasoning tasks (GSM8K).
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly? To study this, we extract activations after a question is read but before any tokens are generated, and train linear probes to predict whether the model's forthcoming answer will be correct. Across three open-source model families ranging from 7 to 70 billion parameters, projections on this "in-advance correctness direction" trained on generic trivia questions predict success in distribution and on diverse out-of-distribution knowledge datasets, indicating a deeper signal than dataset-specific spurious features, and outperforming black-box baselines and verbalised predicted confidence. Predictive power saturates in intermediate layers and, notably, generalisation falters on questions requiring mathematical reasoning. Moreover, for models responding "I don't know", doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, indicating that the same direction also captures confidence. By complementing previous results on truthfulness and other behaviours obtained with probes and sparse auto-encoders, our work contributes essential findings to elucidate LLM internals.

papers.title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models can monitor their own internal states and resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, a phenomenon termed Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR).
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces and characterizes Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), showing that large language models can self-correct during inference when subjected to task-misaligned activation steering, and provides causal evidence for internal consistency-checking circuits.
papers.conclusion: ESR demonstrates that large language models have internal self-monitoring mechanisms that can resist activation steering, which has implications for both robustness and safety, highlighting the need to understand and control these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama-3.3-70B exhibits substantial Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families show it less frequently.
26 SAE latents are identified as off-topic detectors and causally linked to ESR; ablating them reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%.
ESR can be enhanced through meta-prompts, increasing the multi-attempt rate by 4.3× for Llama-3.3-70B.
Fine-tuning on self-correction examples can induce ESR-like behavior in smaller models, but only increases attempt frequency without improving success rate.
ESR has dual implications: it could protect against adversarial manipulation but might interfere with beneficial safety interventions.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on single-layer SAEs limits tracing of inter-layer dynamics.
Only 5 models tested, making it difficult to disentangle effects of scale, architecture, and training.
Judge-based evaluation involves subjective assessment of response quality.
future_direction: Investigate whether ESR emerges from RLHF or exists in pretrained representations.
Study how ESR responds to safety-relevant steering.
Explore whether ESR can be adversarially circumvented.
papers.abstract: Large language models can resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, sometimes recovering mid-generation to produce improved responses even when steering remains active. We term this Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR). Using sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents to steer model activations, we find that Llama-3.3-70B shows substantial ESR, while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families exhibit the phenomenon less frequently. We identify 26 SAE latents that activate differentially during off-topic content and are causally linked to ESR in Llama-3.3-70B. Zero-ablating these latents reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%, providing causal evidence for dedicated internal consistency-checking circuits. We demonstrate that ESR can be deliberately enhanced through both prompting and training: meta-prompts instructing the model to self-monitor increase the multi-attempt rate by 4x for Llama-3.3-70B, and fine-tuning on self-correction examples successfully induces ESR-like behavior in smaller models. These findings have dual implications: ESR could protect against adversarial manipulation but might also interfere with beneficial safety interventions that rely on activation steering. Understanding and controlling these resistance mechanisms is important for developing transparent and controllable AI systems. Code is available at github.com/agencyenterprise/endogenous-steering-resistance.

papers.title: What does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis Have to do with Knowledge?
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis adequately explain the process of factual expression in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification; MLP weights store complex token expression patterns that are linguistically interpretable but do not constitute 'knowledge'.
papers.conclusion: The Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification; MLP neurons store interpretable token expression patterns, not knowledge. A better understanding requires examining the entire transformer circuit, including attention mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic phenomena can be localized to specific neurons using the same gradient-based methods as factual knowledge.
Editing these identified neurons has limited impact on categorical predictions and is influenced by superficial cues like word co-occurrence frequencies.
The ROME model-editing method only superficially alters token association patterns and fails under newly proposed symmetry and synonymy criteria.
The distribution of knowledge neurons for syntactic and factual information is similar, with both occupying the topmost layers of the model.
MLP modules do not store knowledge but rather complex token expression patterns that can be interpreted linguistically.
papers.limitation:
Editing identified knowledge neurons has low reliability and is not strong enough to overturn categorical predictions.
Current circuit identification methods are ad hoc and have only been applied to a small set of tasks.
future_direction: Formalize the circuit interpretation framework and apply it to more tasks and phenomena.
Investigate the entire decision-making circuit beyond MLP modules.
papers.abstract: We reassess the Knowledge Neuron (KN) Thesis: an interpretation of the mechanism underlying the ability of large language models to recall facts from a training corpus. This nascent thesis proposes that facts are recalled from the training corpus through the MLP weights in a manner resembling key-value memory, implying in effect that "knowledge" is stored in the network. Furthermore, by modifying the MLP modules, one can control the language model's generation of factual information. The plausibility of the KN thesis has been demonstrated by the success of KN-inspired model editing methods (Dai et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2022). We find that this thesis is, at best, an oversimplification. Not only have we found that we can edit the expression of certain linguistic phenomena using the same model editing methods but, through a more comprehensive evaluation, we have found that the KN thesis does not adequately explain the process of factual expression. While it is possible to argue that the MLP weights store complex patterns that are interpretable both syntactically and semantically, these patterns do not constitute "knowledge." To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the knowledge representation process, we must look beyond the MLP weights and explore recent models' complex layer structures and attention mechanisms.

papers.title: How do language models learn facts? Dynamics, curricula and hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire factual knowledge during training, and what are the dynamics, the impact of data distribution, and the challenges of integrating new knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-phase learning process for factual recall in language models, shows how data distribution affects dynamics, and demonstrates that fine-tuning to add new knowledge is challenging due to hallucinations and corruption of existing memories.
papers.conclusion: The paper emphasizes the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggests data scheduling strategies to accelerate training, while highlighting the difficulty of integrating new knowledge post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn factual recall in three phases: initial language understanding, a performance plateau, and then knowledge emergence.
The plateau phase corresponds to the development of attention-based recall circuits.
Imbalanced data distributions shorten the plateau but can lead to overfitting.
Hallucinations (overconfident predictions on unseen individuals) emerge simultaneously with knowledge acquisition.
Fine-tuning to incorporate new knowledge quickly corrupts existing parametric memories.
papers.limitation: The results do not rule out that other qualitative changes may occur during the plateau phase, and they do not provide any mechanistic insights regarding how models acquire individual-specific knowledge.
future_direction: Further investigation is needed to better understand the precise conditions under which data repetition can effectively reduce time spent on performance plateaus during training.
The data scheduling strategy could be dynamically adjusted based on observed plateau termination.
papers.abstract: Large language models accumulate vast knowledge during pre-training, yet the dynamics governing this acquisition remain poorly understood. This work investigates the learning dynamics of language models on a synthetic factual recall task, uncovering three key findings: First, language models learn in three phases, exhibiting a performance plateau before acquiring precise factual knowledge. Mechanistically, this plateau coincides with the formation of attention-based circuits that support recall. Second, the training data distribution significantly impacts learning dynamics, as imbalanced distributions lead to shorter plateaus. Finally, hallucinations emerge simultaneously with knowledge, and integrating new knowledge into the model through fine-tuning is challenging, as it quickly corrupts its existing parametric memories. Our results emphasize the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggest novel data scheduling strategies to accelerate neural network training.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that induction heads, through their prefix matching and copying mechanism, are a fundamental component enabling few-shot in-context learning in large language models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating a small percentage (1-3%) of induction heads leads to substantial decreases in ICL performance, much more so than ablating random heads.
Blocking the specific induction attention pattern (via attention knockout) causes performance drops similar to full head ablation, confirming the mechanism's specific role.
The importance of induction heads for ICL holds across abstract pattern recognition tasks and real-world NLP tasks.
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of the prefix matching and copying mechanism to enable pattern matching in ICL.
The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, highlighting their role in learning from examples.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for identifying induction heads, lacking a mechanistic basis for definitive identification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks; further research is required for NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL; other mechanisms may exist.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL). However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking. This paper explores the role of induction heads in a few-shot ICL setting. We analyse two state-of-the-art models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks. Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random. For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts. We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present fine-grained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: Revealing the Deceptiveness of Knowledge Editing: A Mechanistic Analysis of Superficial Editing
papers.research_question: Why do knowledge-edited language models revert to their original knowledge when presented with carefully crafted prompts (attack probes), despite appearing successfully edited according to conventional metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of superficial editing, provides evaluation datasets and metrics, and identifies two key mechanistic factors: the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and specific attention modules in later layers, showing that specific attention heads and their left singular vectors encode original knowledge and cause superficial editing.
papers.conclusion: Superficial editing is a significant challenge for knowledge editing, and the mechanistic analysis reveals the underlying factors in the residual stream and attention modules, with broader applicability to unlearning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect conventional metrics but are vulnerable to attack probes, exhibiting superficial editing in over 70% of cases for some methods.
The residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers shows inhibited enrichment of new knowledge and limited accumulation of original knowledge.
Later attention modules cause the Reversal of the Residual Stream (RRS) phenomenon by incorporating original knowledge into the last position, leading to superficial editing.
Specific attention heads in later layers and their left singular vectors are causally responsible for encoding original knowledge and inducing superficial editing.
Similar patterns are observed in superficial unlearning, demonstrating the generality of the findings.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing, which aims to update the knowledge encoded in language models, can be deceptive. Despite the fact that many existing knowledge editing algorithms achieve near-perfect performance on conventional metrics, the models edited by them are still prone to generating original knowledge. This paper introduces the concept of "superficial editing" to describe this phenomenon. Our comprehensive evaluation reveals that this issue presents a significant challenge to existing algorithms. Through systematic investigation, we identify and validate two key factors contributing to this issue: (1) the residual stream at the last subject position in earlier layers and (2) specific attention modules in later layers. Notably, certain attention heads in later layers, along with specific left singular vectors in their output matrices, encapsulate the original knowledge and exhibit a causal relationship with superficial editing. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to the task of superficial unlearning, where we observe consistent patterns in the behavior of specific attention heads and their corresponding left singular vectors, thereby demonstrating the robustness and broader applicability of our methodology and conclusions. Our code is available here.

papers.title: Walk the Talk? Measuring the Faithfulness of Large Language Model Explanations
papers.research_question: How can we measure the faithfulness of LLM explanations, specifically the alignment between the concepts that explanations imply are influential and those that are truly influential?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for measuring the faithfulness of LLM explanations by comparing the concepts that explanations imply are influential with those that are truly influential, using counterfactual generation and Bayesian hierarchical modeling.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method effectively measures faithfulness and uncovers semantic patterns of unfaithfulness, which can inform users and developers about LLM limitations and mitigate risks of over-trust.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-3.5 produces more faithful explanations than GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet on a social bias task.
LLM explanations can hide social bias (e.g., gender, race) and the influence of safety measures.
On a medical question answering task, LLM explanations provide misleading claims about which pieces of evidence influenced decisions.
Smaller models like Llama-3.1-8B can be more faithful than larger models.
The method reveals category-specific patterns of unfaithfulness, such as over-referencing behavior concepts and under-referencing identity concepts.
papers.limitation: Reliance on an auxiliary LLM for concept extraction and counterfactual generation may introduce errors.
future_direction: Explore alternative methods for concept extraction and counterfactual generation.
Apply the method to more domains and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are capable of generating plausible explanations of how they arrived at an answer to a question. However, these explanations can misrepresent the model's "reasoning" process, i.e., they can be unfaithful. This, in turn, can lead to over-trust and misuse. We introduce a new approach for measuring the faithfulness of LLM explanations. First, we provide a rigorous definition of faithfulness. Since LLM explanations mimic human explanations, they often reference high-level concepts in the input question that purportedly influenced the model. We define faithfulness in terms of the difference between the set of concepts that LLM explanations imply are influential and the set that truly are. Second, we present a novel method for estimating faithfulness that is based on: (1) using an auxiliary LLM to modify the values of concepts within model inputs to create realistic counterfactuals, and (2) using a Bayesian hierarchical model to quantify the causal effects of concepts at both the example- and dataset-level. Our experiments show that our method can be used to quantify and discover interpretable patterns of unfaithfulness. On a social bias task, we uncover cases where LLM explanations hide the influence of social bias. On a medical question answering task, we uncover cases where LLM explanations provide misleading claims about which pieces of evidence influenced the model's decisions.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Acquire New Knowledge? A Knowledge Circuits Perspective on Continual Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) structurally embed and acquire new knowledge during continual pre-training, from the perspective of knowledge circuit evolution?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the evolution of knowledge circuits during continual pre-training, revealing that new knowledge acquisition is influenced by relevance to existing knowledge, follows a biphasic (formation then optimization) pattern, and exhibits a deep-to-shallow component evolution.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the theoretical understanding of new knowledge acquisition mechanisms in LLMs and provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The acquisition of new knowledge is significantly influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge, with relevant new knowledge being integrated more efficiently than completely new knowledge.
The evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization, each marked by unique structural and behavioral characteristics.
The evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern, where mid-to-deeper layers first develop the extraction function, and later, lower layers enrich their knowledge representations.
The performance of knowledge circuits is positively correlated with knowledge frequency, with low-frequency knowledge circuits suffering from insufficient representations rather than fundamental capacity limitations.
The state of knowledge circuits could serve as a valuable tracking status for the continual pre-training process, enabling more informed adjustments to training.
future_direction: Utilizing data curriculums in continual pre-training to mimic the structure of the original corpus for more efficient integration.
Using the state of knowledge circuits as a tracking status to enable informed adjustments to training methods or data in response to different phases.
Further investigation into knowledge capacity scaling laws and their impact on model behavior during continual pre-training.
papers.abstract: Despite exceptional capabilities in knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) face a critical gap in understanding how they internalize new knowledge, particularly how to structurally embed acquired knowledge in their neural computations. We address this issue through the lens of knowledge circuit evolution, identifying computational subgraphs that facilitate knowledge storage and processing. Our systematic analysis of circuit evolution throughout continual pre-training reveals several key findings: (1) the acquisition of new knowledge is influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge; (2) the evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization; (3) the evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern. These insights not only advance our theoretical understanding of the mechanisms of new knowledge acquisition in LLMs, but also provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/zjunlp/DynamicKnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: Delving into the Reversal Curse: How Far Can Large Language Models Generalize?
papers.research_question: How does the reversal curse manifest across various tasks, and what are the underlying generalization abilities and problem-solving mechanisms of LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that the reversal curse is more likely a backward recall deficiency, and identifies an inherent 'thinking bias' in LLMs where they preferentially use names to initiate fact recall, which strongly influences their generalization ability based on training data structure.
papers.conclusion: The reversal curse is a backward recall deficiency in decoder-only models, and LLMs' inherent thinking bias underscores the critical importance of appropriate training data structure for successful knowledge application and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can generalize to 'B is A' when both A and B are presented in context (e.g., in multiple-choice questions).
Generalization ability is highly correlated with the structure of training documents (works for '[Name] is [Description]' but not the reverse).
LLMs possess an inherent thinking bias: they consistently start fact recall with names provided in the query.
The negative impact of this bias on downstream task performance is hard to mitigate through training alone.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) showcase unprecedented capabilities, they also exhibit certain inherent limitations when facing seemingly trivial tasks. A prime example is the recently debated "reversal curse", which surfaces when models, having been trained on the fact "A is B", struggle to generalize this knowledge to infer that "B is A". In this paper, we examine the manifestation of the reversal curse across various tasks and delve into both the generalization abilities and the problem-solving mechanisms of LLMs. This investigation leads to a series of significant insights: (1) LLMs are able to generalize to "B is A" when both A and B are presented in the context as in the case of a multiple-choice question. (2) This generalization ability is highly correlated to the structure of the fact "A is B" in the training documents. For example, this generalization only applies to biographies structured in "[Name] is [Description]" but not to "[Description] is [Name]". (3) We propose and verify the hypothesis that LLMs possess an inherent bias in fact recalling during knowledge application, which explains and underscores the importance of the document structure to successful learning. (4) The negative impact of this bias on the downstream performance of LLMs can hardly be mitigated through training alone. These findings offer a novel perspective on interpreting LLMs' generalization through their intrinsic mechanisms and provide insights for developing more effective learning methods. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/alibaba/thinking_bias.git.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of knowledge neurons and a gradient-based attribution method to identify them in pretrained Transformers, demonstrating their role in storing factual knowledge and enabling model editing.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons (knowledge neurons) within feed-forward networks, and these neurons can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed attribution method are positively correlated with the expression of specific factual knowledge.
Suppressing or amplifying the activation of identified knowledge neurons significantly decreases or increases the probability of the correct answer, respectively.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts expressing their corresponding fact than by control prompts.
Knowledge neurons can be used to update or erase specific factual knowledge in the model with minimal impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Examines knowledge neurons based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain underexplored.
Focuses on factual knowledge for ease of evaluation, though the method is applicable to other knowledge types.
Uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Explore interactions between knowledge neurons.
Extend the method to other types of knowledge beyond factual knowledge.
Extend to multi-word blanks in cloze queries.
Investigate knowledge neurons in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus. In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models: 'truth directions' are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context affect the truth-value probes in large language models, and are these probes coherently incorporating contextual information?
papers.core_contribution: Truth-value probes are context sensitive but also sensitive to irrelevant information, and truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference.
papers.conclusion: Truth-value directions are context sensitive and causally mediate inference, but probes are not fully coherent.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-value probes are sensitive to context, but also to irrelevant information.
The type of errors (consistency errors) depend on the layer, model, and data.
Probes trained without premises (no-prem) still show context sensitivity, indicating that prior beliefs are not represented independently.
Instruction-tuned models show different error patterns (more E4 errors) compared to pretrained-only models.
Truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference (intervention experiment).
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as uncovering a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions are (most) sensitive to the presence of related sentences, and how to best characterize this kind of sensitivity. We do so by measuring different types of consistency errors that occur after probing an LLM whose inputs consist of hypotheses preceded by (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these truth-value directions influences the position of an entailed or contradicted sentence along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that truth-value directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Towards Tracing Knowledge in Language Models Back to the Training Data
papers.research_question: How can we identify which training examples taught a language model to generate a particular factual assertion?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the problem of fact tracing and presents the first quantitative benchmark (FTRACE) to evaluate training data attribution methods for tracing factual knowledge in language models back to specific training examples.
papers.conclusion: Significant headroom remains for improving training data attribution methods for fact tracing, with key challenges including gradient saturation and the importance of nuanced implementation details.
papers.key_findings:
Current TDA methods (gradient-based TRACIN and embedding-based EMBED) underperform a simple IR baseline (BM25) on the natural fact tracing benchmark (FTRACE-TREx).
On the controlled synthetic benchmark (FTRACE-SYNTH), TDA methods show better upper bounds, indicating potential when lexical overlap is reduced.
Optimizing TDA hyperparameters (e.g., layer selection, gradient normalization, using optimizer accumulators) significantly improves performance.
The embedding layer provides the most reliable attribution signal for both gradient and embedding-based methods.
Gradient saturation is a key challenge for TDA methods when facts are already known by the model.
papers.limitation:
Gradient saturation: when a model already knows a fact, gradients are near zero, making it difficult for TDA methods to attribute.
The natural benchmark (FTRACE-TREx) may have lexical overlap that favors surface-level IR methods like BM25.
future_direction: Improving TDA methods to overcome the gradient saturation problem.
Better handling of indirect proponents (facts inferred from other facts).
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) have been shown to memorize a great deal of factual knowledge contained in their training data. But when an LM generates an assertion, it is often difficult to determine where it learned this information and whether it is true. In this paper, we propose the problem of fact tracing: identifying which training examples taught an LM to generate a particular factual assertion. Prior work on training data attribution (TDA) may offer effective tools for identifying such examples, known as “proponents”. We present the first quantitative benchmark to evaluate this. We compare two popular families of TDA methods — gradient-based and embedding-based — and find that much headroom remains. For example, both methods have lower proponent-retrieval precision than an information retrieval baseline (BM25) that does not have access to the LM at all. We identify key challenges that may be necessary for further improvement such as overcoming the problem of gradient saturation, and also show how several nuanced implementation details of existing neural TDA methods can significantly improve overall fact tracing performance.

papers.title: LLM Knowledge is Brittle: Truthfulness Representations Rely on Superficial Resemblance
papers.research_question: Do LLMs learn robust underlying knowledge representations, or are they fragile and tied to the exact phrasings and formulations seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs' internal representations of statement truthfulness are brittle and degrade under superficial, semantically-preserving transformations, indicating that knowledge representations rely on superficial resemblance to pre-training data rather than robust, generalizable knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LLMs learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that fail to generalize to scenarios unlike those seen during training, presenting a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes and the reliability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness separability degrades as samples become more out-of-distribution (OOD) across all probing methods, datasets, and model families.
Certain topics (e.g., sociology, marketing) have more robust representations than others (e.g., history).
Benchmark performance does not imply robust representations; knowledge representations degrade even for questions the model answers correctly.
Larger models may not be more robust; the 70B Llama model showed the steepest degradation in some cases.
The type of transformation affects degradation differently; translation breaks representations while negation does not affect internal probe performance.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to decoder-only autoregressive language models.
Use of perplexity as a proxy for out-of-distribution (OOD) may not be perfect.
Only semantically-preserving transformations are considered.
future_direction: Improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.
Extending the analysis to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder models).
Exploring other types of distribution shifts beyond superficial transformations.
papers.abstract: For Large Language Models (LLMs) to be reliable, they must learn robust knowledge that can be generally applied in diverse settings -- often unlike those seen during training. Yet, extensive research has shown that LLM performance can be brittle, with models exhibiting excessive sensitivity to trivial input variations. In this work, we explore whether this brittleness is a direct result of unstable internal knowledge representations. To explore this question, we build on previous work showing that LLM representations encode statement truthfulness -- i.e., true, factual statements can be easily separated from false, inaccurate ones. Specifically, we test the robustness of learned knowledge by evaluating representation separability on samples that have undergone superficial transformations to drive them out-of-distribution (OOD), such as typos or reformulations. By applying semantically-preserving perturbations, we study how separability degrades as statements become more OOD, across four LLM families, five evaluation datasets, and three knowledge probing methods. Our results reveal that internal representations of statement truthfulness collapse as the samples' presentations become less similar to those seen during pre-training. While LLMs can often distinguish between true and false statements when they closely resemble the pre-training data, this ability is highly dependent on the statement's exact surface form. These findings offer a possible explanation for brittle benchmark performance: LLMs may learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that allow for only limited generalizability. Our work presents a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes, and more broadly, calls for further research on improving the robustness of learned knowledge representations.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: Structural Persistence in Language Models: Priming as a Window into Abstract Language Representations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that Transformer language models are susceptible to structural priming, revealing they encode abstract structural information that is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, and may involve hierarchical syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer language models show evidence of structural priming.
Priming strength is boosted by semantic similarity and lexical overlap between prime and target sentences.
Priming effects persist but are asymmetrical when primes are semantically implausible.
Priming strength increases with recency (proximity) and cumulative exposure to the prime structure.
The structural representations may encode hierarchical syntactic information, as shown by priming with nested dependencies.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on only two syntactic alternations in English.
The corpus is template-based and may not capture naturalistic language.
Only auto-regressive language models are considered; masked LMs are not investigated.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other syntactic constructions and languages.
Use more naturalistic data beyond template-based corpora.
Investigate structural priming in masked language models.
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigate the extent to which modern neural language models are susceptible to structural priming, the phenomenon whereby the structure of a sentence makes the same structure more probable in a follow-up sentence. We explore how priming can be used to study the potential of these models to learn abstract structural information, which is a prerequisite for good performance on tasks that require natural language understanding skills. We introduce a novel metric and release Prime-LM, a large corpus where we control for various linguistic factors that interact with priming strength. We find that Transformer models indeed show evidence of structural priming, but also that the generalizations they learned are to some extent modulated by semantic information. Our experiments also show that the representations acquired by the models may not only encode abstract sequential structure but involve certain level of hierarchical syntactic information. More generally, our study shows that the priming paradigm is a useful, additional tool for gaining insights into the capacities of language models and opens the door to future priming-based investigations that probe the model’s internal states.1

papers.title: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand the mechanism of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify task-detection and task-execution features in the in-context learning circuit of large language models, and introduces the Task Vector Cleaning algorithm to decompose task vectors into interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of in-context learning mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders as a powerful tool for interpretability research on larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be used to analyze in-context learning in larger models like Gemma-1 2B, scaling up circuit analysis.
Task-execution features encode task knowledge and can causally induce task zero-shot performance.
Task-detection features identify tasks from the prompt and are causally linked to execution features via attention and MLP sublayers.
The Task Vector Cleaning algorithm effectively decomposes task vectors into sparse, interpretable features while preserving their effect on loss.
The in-context learning circuit involves interaction between detection and execution features through attention and MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Circuit search was constrained to intermediate layers due to early layers processing token-level information and having lower quality Indirect Effect approximations.
Hundreds of features needed to be ablated to achieve significant faithfulness degradation, unlike prior work which required fewer.
Negative steering experiments showed lower task specificity, indicating steering experiments alone may not suffice for comprehensive analysis.
future_direction: Improving SAE training to yield more monosemantic features.
Scaling circuit analysis to even larger models.
Applying these techniques to more complex tasks.
